topic: •Introduction to the Document Object Model (DOM) and why JavaScript uses it. •Finding HTML elements with document.getElementById(). •Changing content using textContent and innerHTML. •Changing CSS styles using JavaScript (style.color, style.backgroundColor). •Linking an external JavaScript file to an HTML page. •Introduction to JavaScript Events.
summary:
This session opened a new module covering the DOM, DOM Events, APIs, async/await, and ES6+ (the modern JavaScript standard introduced in 2015 and updated every year since). Today's class focused specifically on the DOM: what it is, and how JavaScript uses it to change text, styles, and images, show or hide elements, create or remove elements, respond to clicks, and read information from forms.

The student was introduced to document.getElementById() as the standard way to locate an element by its id, and saw how it can be combined with innerHTML and textContent to change what appears on the page. A further example showed how JavaScript can change an element's appearance directly using style.color and style.backgroundColor.

The class then covered how to move JavaScript out of the HTML file and into a separate external script.js file, linked using <script src="script.js"></script>. To close, JavaScript events were introduced as a lead-in to the next topic – anything that “happens” on a page, such as a click, a keystroke, a form submission, or a page load – which JavaScript can be written to respond to.

To reinforce the session, the student was given the following assignment:
Assignment: Research the difference between a website and a web app (web application), and read about page types such as parent/menu pages and child/sub-menu pages.
tutorRemark: Today's class introduced the DOM, a significant step up that opens the door to real interactivity on webpages. We covered the core methods for finding and changing elements, alongside a first look at external JavaScript files and events. I'd encourage continued practice with document.getElementById(), textContent, and innerHTML at home to build fluency before we move further into DOM Events next session.

topic: Application Programming Interface (API), fetch(), JSON, and HTTP Status Codes  The class focused on introducing the student to APIs and how JavaScript can communicate with external services to retrieve and display information on a webpage.
summary:
The class began with assignment checking, and the student completed the assignment correctly, demonstrating a good understanding of the concepts covered in the previous lesson, and the project image was shown to her and has been sent to her, and the project guide will be given to her next class.

The lesson then introduced an API (Application Programming Interface). The student learned that an API allows one program or application to communicate with another program or service. A simple real-world example of a weather application requesting weather information from a weather API was used to make the concept easier to understand.

Practical examples were demonstrated using JavaScript's fetch() method. The student learned how a webpage can request information from an online API and use the returned information on the webpage.

Several API examples were explored, including:

- A general data API using JSONPlaceholder.
- A Weather API for retrieving temperature and wind-speed information.
- An Image API for displaying random dog images.
- A Student/School API example for retrieving and displaying user information.

The student was also introduced to JSON (JavaScript Object Notation) and learned that JSON is a common format used for sending and receiving data between applications and APIs.

The following flow was explained:

JavaScript → fetch() → API → JSON Data → JavaScript → Webpage

The student also learned the basic structure of JSON using keys and values, such as:

name → John
age → 15
country → Nigeria

The use of:

response.json()

was explained as the process of converting the API response into JavaScript data that can be used by the application.

The lesson also introduced HTTP status codes, including the meaning of common codes such as 200 (successful request) and 404 (resource not found), to help the student understand how a browser or application can know whether an API request was successful or encountered a problem.
tutorRemark: The student performed well during the assignment review and was able to proceed successfully into the new topic of APIs.  The practical examples helped demonstrate how JavaScript can be used to retrieve text, weather information, images, and other data from external services. The student was encouraged to continue practising fetch(), JSON, and displaying API data using the DOM.  Two assignments were given to reinforce the lesson:  Assignment 1: Fetch information from three different APIs/websites using HTML, CSS, and JavaScript and display the returned information on the webpage.  Assignment 2: Study the common HTTP status codes and their meanings, with particular attention to codes such as 200, 201, 400, 401, 403, 404, 500, and 503.  Overall, the student showed good progress and is beginning to understand how JavaScript can communicate with external services and use the received data to create interactive web applications.

topic: Node.js, Express.js and Database (PostgreSQL)  The class introduced the student to the fundamentals of backend web development using Node.js, Express.js, and PostgreSQL.  The following concepts were covered:  Node.js – A JavaScript runtime that allows JavaScript to run outside the web browser and is commonly used for server-side development. Express.js – A Node.js framework used to create web servers, backend applications, and API routes. PostgreSQL – A relational database system used to store, manage, and retrieve application data. Understanding the relationship between the three technologies: Node.js → The engine/runtime Express.js → The server/backend framework PostgreSQL → The database/storage system Installation of the LTS version of Node.js. Understanding npm (Node Package Manager) and its purpose in installing and managing Node.js packages. Checking Node.js and npm installation using: node --version npm --version Introduction to creating a backend project using VS Code. Creating a package.json file using: npm init -y Installing Express.js using: npm install express Checking the installed Express version using: npm list express Understanding the purpose of: node_modules package.json package-lock.json Introduction to PostgreSQL installation and the PostgreSQL VS Code extension. Installing the PostgreSQL Node.js package using: npm install pg Understanding the use of the pg package for connecting Node.js applications to PostgreSQL databases. Checking PostgreSQL installation using: psql --version Understanding how Express and PostgreSQL packages appear under the project's dependencies.
summary:
The class focused on introducing the student to backend development with Node.js and Express.js, together with database management using PostgreSQL.

The student learned that Node.js provides the environment for executing JavaScript on the server, while Express.js can be used to build the backend server and API routes. PostgreSQL was introduced as the database where application information can be permanently stored and managed.

The student was also guided through the initial setup of a backend project in VS Code. This included creating a project folder named backend-project, initializing the project with npm init -y, installing Express.js, and understanding the files and folders automatically created by npm.

The class further introduced PostgreSQL and the pg Node.js package, which will allow the backend application to communicate with the PostgreSQL database.

By the end of the lesson, the student had an understanding of the basic backend architecture:

Client/Browser → Express.js → Node.js → PostgreSQL Database
tutorRemark: The student was introduced to important backend development concepts and successfully learned the roles of Node.js, Express.js, and PostgreSQL in a modern web application.  The student demonstrated an understanding of the purpose of npm, project initialization, package installation, and the basic structure of a Node.js backend project. The introduction to PostgreSQL also provided a good foundation for understanding how backend applications interact with databases.  The next stage will be focused on creating the Express server, connecting Node.js to PostgreSQL to display if the server, framework and database are working.

topic: JWT Authentication and Authorization (Header, Payload, Signature)  Express & PostgreSQL Integration  Password Hashing with Bcrypt  Project Assignment: Student Management System (Deployment to Railway)
summary:
The session focused on securing Node.js/Express applications using JSON Web Tokens (JWT) and PostgreSQL. Key concepts included the 3-part token structure, safe payload handling (avoiding plain-text sensitive data), and the end-to-end authentication lifecycle using Express middleware. Practical implementation covered essential npm packages (express, pg, jsonwebtoken, bcrypt/bcryptjs, dotenv), designing a secure users table schema, and hashing passwords before database storage. 

The class concluded with assigning a Student Management System project to be deployed on Railway.
tutorRemark: Well done today. Student understood how login tokens and password security work, and the database setup was clear, and the student should Keep the momentum going as She build and deploy the Student Management System to Railway.

topic: Building a secure backend authentication system using Express, PostgreSQL, and JSON Web Tokens (JWT).
summary:
The session focused on setting up essential dependencies (express, pg, jsonwebtoken, bcryptjs, dotenv, and nodemon) and organizing a modular project directory separating server setup, database configuration, auth routes, and static client files. 

The end-to-end authentication lifecycle was established: hashing passwords with bcryptjs for registration into PostgreSQL, validating credentials and issuing JWTs upon login, and enforcing authorization on protected routes via token verification middleware.
tutorRemark: The core architectural flow is solid and shows a clear grasp of stateless token authentication. To make this production-ready, ensure PostgreSQL queries always use parameterized inputs ($1, $2) to block SQL injection, set explicit token expiration times, and store JWTs in HttpOnly cookies to protect against XSS vulnerabilities.
